evidence.text: water
Phonosemantic compound. 氵 represents the meaning and 青 represents the sound.
朖也。澂水之皃。从水青聲。

Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *sʰleŋ): semantic 氵 (“water”) + phonetic 青 (OC *sʰleːŋ).
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *(t)s(j)aŋ (“clear; pure; clean”); cognate with Tibetan གཙང (gtsang, “clean; pure”), Mizo thiang (“to be clear; to be clean; to be pure”), Southern Qiang ɕó, Drung cangma (“clean”), Burmese စင် (cang, “clean, pure”) (Schuessler, 2007; STEDT).
Within Chinese, cognate with 淨 (OC *zeŋs, “clean”), 醒 (OC *seːŋ, *seːŋʔ, *seːŋs, “to wake up; to become sober”), and allofamic with 星 (OC *sleːŋ, “star”), 晴 (OC *zleŋ, “(of weather) clear; fine”); possibly also related to 靜 (OC *zleŋʔ, “quiet”) (Schuessler, 2007).
Perhaps an areal word; compare Proto-Mon-Khmer *caŋ (“to glitter”) (Schuessler, 2007).
Rebracketing of the reading of Ching, which is a nonstandard romanisation of 師兄 /师兄 (si¹ hing¹).
朖也。澂水之皃。从水青聲。

Bronze and manuscript forms combine 水 with phonetic 青. The original meaning concerns clear water. Manuscript uses include pure wine and a borrowing for 靜, quiet.
evidence.title: 清 — historical form and meaning

evidence.text: Water began as a flowing-water picture. In a side position its compressed, stylized form is 氵; this form is unrelated to 冫.
evidence.title: 水 — glyph origin

evidence.text: Ordinary Mandarin color reading: qīng; another listed reading is jīng in a separate usage.
evidence.title: 青 — Mandarin pronunciation

evidence.text: The pronunciation table explicitly labels 青 *sʰleːŋ as Old Chinese in the Zhengzhang (2003) system.
evidence.title: 青 — Old Chinese pronunciation

evidence.field: 形義源流通解; 金文、簡帛用例
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 清 as 水 meaning plus 青 sound, with the original sense “clear water.” It says the bronze inscription meaning is uncertain; it cites the Qin Shuihudi *Rishu* slip phrase 肥豚清酒美白粱 for “pure/mellow wine,” and a Guodian *Laozi* slip use 清清借 for 靜 “quiet/still.” These later textual examples document uses, not the date the senses arose.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 清

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, quoting 《說文解字》 and Duan Yucai’s commentary
evidence.text: The received Shuowen entry glosses 清 as 朖也 and 澂水之皃, and analyzes it as 从水青聲. Duan Yucai interprets 朖 as 明 “bright,” then explicitly describes an extension to 潔 “clean/pure,” including cleansing a person. The entry gives 七情切. This is a historical lexicographic account, not independent proof of the graph’s origin or a dated first attestation.
evidence.title: 說文解字「清」

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 字形、讀音、歷代詞義例證
evidence.text: The entry classifies 清 under 水 and 青, records variant 淸 and other forms, and gives Mandarin qīng. It cites 《詩經·魏風·伐檀》河水清且漣猗 as an example of clear water, then lists uses including purity, cleansing, settling accounts, quiet, peace, and the Qing dynasty. The dictionary’s collected glosses do not by themselves establish the chronology or semantic links among those uses.
evidence.title: A02224 清 — 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Institute of History and Philology, Academia Sinica, Character Database
evidence.text: The 水 entry presents oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript, and seal-script categories and describes 水 as a pictograph of the winding, undulating shape of flowing water. It supports the history of the semantic component itself; it is not direct evidence for a specific early 清 allograph.
evidence.title: 漢字「水」：字形演變

evidence.field: 清 Old Chinese and Middle Chinese readings
evidence.text: The page lists modern Beijing Mandarin qīng and Middle Chinese tshjeng. It gives two Old Chinese reconstructions: Baxter–Sagart /*tsʰeŋ/ (system 1.1, 2014) and Zhengzhang /*sʰleŋ/ (2003). The discrepancy reflects different reconstruction systems; these are scholarly reconstructions, not direct recordings.

evidence.field: 青 sound component; Old Chinese pronunciation
evidence.text: The page associates 青 with the 生 phonetic series and lists Zhengzhang (2003) Old Chinese /*sʰleːŋ/ for 青. Compared in that same reconstruction system with 清 /*sʰleŋ/, this is a close sound correspondence consistent with 青 functioning as a phonetic component. 青’s listed Baxter–Sagart form is /*[s.r̥]ˤeŋ/.
evidence.title: 青 — Wiktionary

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Revised Mandarin Dictionary
evidence.text: The entry gives 青 readings qīng and jīng, with qīng as the reading for its color sense and jīng cross-referenced to a separate usage. This confirms the component’s ordinary modern reading but does not establish the reading at the time 清 was formed.

evidence.text: Its 水 entry describes the graph as a flowing-water pictograph and says the side-position 氵 is a compressed stylized form. This is consistent with reading 清’s left component as water semantics, not as 冫. The modern three-dot form alone does not document the dated stages of 清’s own graphic development.

evidence.text: The page proposes a Proto-Sino-Tibetan comparison *(t)s(j)aŋ ‘clear; pure; clean’ and compares Tibetan gtsang, Mizo thiang, Southern Qiang ɕó, Drung cangma, and Burmese cang, citing Schuessler (2007) and STEDT. This is a lexical etymology proposal about the spoken word, distinct from 清’s graph formation; the inspected entry does not supply dated early attestations or enough primary comparative documentation to independently establish the cognacy.

evidence.field: 清: graph categories, Shuowen analysis, historical use reports
evidence.text: The entry labels one small-seal, two bronze, and fifteen manuscript forms. It analyzes 清 as 水 plus phonetic 青, describes its original sense as clear water, and says the bronze examples’ meaning is unclear. It reports 清酒 in the Shuihudi Qin *Rishu* and 清清(靜)為天下定 in Guodian *Laozi*乙. These are the dictionary’s identifications and reports; the linked glyph images and manuscript plates were not visually inspected.

evidence.source: 說文.org, received 說文解字 with Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.field: Received gloss, formation, fanqie, and commentary
evidence.text: The received entry says 清 means 朖 and describes the appearance of clear water; it analyzes the graph as 从水青聲 and gives 七情切. Duan Yucai interprets 朖 as 明 and proposes an extension to 潔, including cleansing a person. This is a historical lexicographic interpretation, not a dated attestation or independently established semantic sequence.

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 清: received Shuowen, dictionary citations and senses
evidence.text: The entry gives the received Shuowen component analysis and the reading qīng. It cites 河水清且漣猗 from the transmitted 《詩經·魏風·伐檀》, among later examples for purity, cleansing, quiet, and peace. The cited Shijing passage is evidence of a transmitted textual use, but not proof of the earliest occurrence; the glossary does not establish a chronology among senses.
evidence.title: A02224 清 — 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.text: The entry lists modern Beijing Mandarin qīng, Middle Chinese tshjeng, Baxter–Sagart (2014, system 1.1) Old Chinese /*tsʰeŋ/, and Zhengzhang (2003) Old Chinese /*sʰleŋ/. These are readings or system-dependent reconstructions, not direct recordings from the time the graph was formed.
evidence.title: 清 — Wiktionary

evidence.source: Wiktionary, Chinese character entries 清 and 青
evidence.text: In the Zhengzhang (2003) Old Chinese reconstruction system, 清 is *sʰleŋ and 青 is *sʰleːŋ. This close same-system correspondence, together with the Shuowen analysis, supports 青’s phonetic role. It is a reconstruction-based inference, not a period pronunciation record. The same table gives 清 and 靜 as *sʰleŋ and *zleŋʔ respectively, so it does not by itself establish the sound basis for the reported 清-for-靜 manuscript spelling.
evidence.title: 清 — Wiktionary

evidence.text: The entry lists modern Beijing Mandarin qīng and Zhengzhang (2003) Old Chinese *sʰleːŋ for 青; it places 青 in the 生 phonetic series. The Mandarin sound is modern, and the Old Chinese form is reconstructed, not contemporaneously recorded.

context.provenance: Base evidence was imported from local JSONL records; those extracts may lose sense or language boundaries. Newly consulted external pages are identified separately with URL, title, access date, and concise paraphrases. Research audit records page access and remaining limits; no independent glyph inspection is claimed.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: No date or catalogued image for the earliest 清 inscription was established from the inspected pages. CUHK reports bronze forms but explicitly says their use is unclear; its images were not visually inspected.
No direct dated attestation for the adjective 清 meaning clear water was established here. The cited 《詩經·魏風·伐檀》 example is a transmitted text, not a demonstrated earliest occurrence.

The cited Qin Shuihudi and Guodian examples are secondary reports in the CUHK entry; their original manuscript editions and archaeological dating were not independently consulted. The semantic path from water clarity to pure wine and to 靜 is plausible from reported uses but not demonstrated as a dated sequence.

The expansion from clear water to general clean/pure is asserted in Duan Yucai’s commentary; intermediate attestations and chronology were not established. Other modern dictionary senses likewise cannot be arranged chronologically from their gloss lists.

青 is identified as phonetic by Shuowen and CUHK. The inspected sources establish modern qīng/jīng and give historical reconstructions for 青 and 清, but no contemporaneous pronunciation record exists; comparative reconstructions are model-dependent.

The Proto-Sino-Tibetan cognacy is a secondary proposal. Independent primary comparative sources and dated attestations for the compared language forms were not inspected, so it remains unverified here.

No specific graph corruption or alternate formation analysis was found in the inspected sources. The supplied pipeline metadata identifying 生 as 青’s phonetic element was not independently validated beyond Wiktionary’s classification of 青 in the 生 phonetic series.

A supplied dossier item refers to a Cantonese rebracketing of Ching as an unrelated slang etymology. It concerns another lexical use and does not explain the Chinese character 清’s formation; that claim was outside the verified character-history evidence.

No candidate could be established with both accessible image contents and verified reuse rights. The CUHK direct links have source-page category labels, but the image resources were inaccessible to the web reader and their reuse terms were not established; they are therefore not proposed as selected glyphs.
No Commons file specifically depicting 清 with supported identity and reuse provenance was found in the inspected search results. This does not establish that none exists elsewhere.

CUHK’s page calls examples 金文 but does not provide, in the inspected accessible text, individual artifact identifiers or dates for each linked bronze image. Its entry states that the bronze usage is unclear.

No glyph pixels were visually inspected. Modern redrawings must not be represented as photographs of ancient artifacts. The linked CUHK image candidates could be redrawings or reproductions, but their status could not be verified.

The reported use of 清 to write 靜 is evidence of a graph spelling in the Guodian manuscript as interpreted by CUHK and a search-result transcription, but the borrowing's phonetic rationale was not independently established: no accessible primary edition or reliable same-system reconstruction comparison for both 清 and 靜 was inspected. It should not be represented as a demonstrated sound-based loan without that comparison.

CUHK reports 清酒 in a Shuihudi Qin manuscript but does not provide an independently inspected manuscript image or primary edition in this research. The Fudan review confirms excavation and publication context for the corpus, not this individual reading or gloss.
The earliest occurrence of adjective 清 meaning clear water remains unresolved. A transmitted Shijing example and the CUHK statement about original meaning do not by themselves date the first use.

No verified graphic sequence or corruption account was established. Secondary paleographic listings identify possible bronze and manuscript examples, but their images and individual identifications were not visually checked.

The proposed Proto-Sino-Tibetan lexical relationship in the supplied dossier was not independently researched in comparative primary sources; it remains a separate, unresolved spoken-word etymology and does not establish graph formation.

No historical glyph is proposed: although source indexes list candidate 清 forms, no candidate was established with a direct image URL, independently verified image identity, individual artifact provenance, and reusable rights.

The Guodian Laozi A transcription inspected does not support the specific claim that 清 writes 靜 in the cited “settle turbidity” passage; it transcribes the graph as 束（静） and then 徐清. The broader reported 清-for-靜 use attributed to CUHK remains unverified against a primary edition here.

The indexed者減鐘 candidate is not individually tied here to a verified glyph image or the museum record for the vessel. The museum page inspected concerns a modern calligraphic transcription, not the original artifact image.

The received Shuowen wording supports a clear-water description. “Bright” comes from Duan Yucai’s interpretation of 朖, not a separately established historical sense; his proposed extension from brightness to cleanliness has no dated intermediate evidence in the inspected sources.

The dossier’s Guodian 清-for-靜 spelling remains disputed: CUHK reports 清清(靜)為天下定, while the opened transcription of Laozi乙 reads 清靜，為天下正. The original manuscript plates and a specialist collation of this specific graph were not inspected, so neither the loan spelling nor its phonetic rationale is established here.

The earliest attestation of 清 meaning clear water remains undated. Calling clear water an original meaning reflects historical lexicographic analysis, not proof that a particular surviving text is the earliest occurrence.
No primary manuscript edition was independently opened for the CUHK-reported Qin Shuihudi 清酒 example; its precise reading and gloss remain secondary-source reports.

No glyph is proposed because no candidate had accessible image content, verified individual provenance, and a reuse license. The discovered secondary index is not itself permission to reuse its images; its rights notice points back to original publications and rightsholders.

The cited ancient-form image links inferred from the secondary page failed to open. No image pixels were inspected; do not represent any candidate as an ancient artifact photograph or as a verified modern redraw.

The CUHK report of 清 borrowing for 靜 remains disputed against the opened Guodian transcription cited in the dossier. No new primary manuscript collation or comparative reconstruction for 靜 was obtained, so neither the precise spelling nor sound basis can be asserted.
The Guodian 清-for-靜 reading has differing editorial transcriptions. The manuscript graph itself and the exact reading were not verified against a primary plate or specialist collation opened in full.

In Zhengzhang (2003), the listed reconstructions 清 *sʰleŋ and 靜 *zleŋʔ differ in initial voicing and tone; the proposed spelling cannot be explained here as an established sound loan from those forms alone. No independently supported reconstruction comparison in another system was obtained for this specific borrowing claim.
CUHK’s Shuihudi 清酒 reading and gloss remain a secondary report; no primary edition or manuscript image was inspected to independently establish the character or the sense.
